explanations.explanation: That's her story: “We were alone, with no one in the house but the two of us.” By her account, it's just the two women in that house. It's her word against the other woman's word. Keep that in mind, because it's what makes this case so tricky.
She says they were alone. Her words are “We were alone, with no one in the house but the two of us.” By her account, it was only the two women. That's why this case is going to be hard to sort out.

explanations.answer: Swapped her dead son for the living one
explanations.explanation: That's what the first woman claims. She says the other woman got up in the middle of the night, took her son from her side while she slept, and put her own dead son in his place. Notice whose side this is: the other woman hasn't had her say yet. I think a swap in the dark is something you'd only catch in the morning light, but that's my guess.

explanations.answer: Hid her dead son outside the house
explanations.explanation: She never mentions anything going outside. She says the other woman “…put her dead son at my bosom.” So in her telling, the dead baby is laid right beside her. It's a heavy picture, and I think it hurts to hear.

explanations.answer: Woke the first woman up for help
explanations.explanation: The first woman says she was asleep when it happened. In her words, the other woman “…took my son from my side while I was asleep.” Her story has no 'hey, I need a hand over here' in it.

Not quite, because there's no confession anywhere in this passage. The first woman says she got up to nurse her son and found him dead. Then she looked closely and realized he was not the son she had borne (1 Kings 3:21). She worked it out with her own eyes, and the other woman never owns up to anything.

Right, no confession here. The first woman says she got up in the morning to nurse her son and found him dead. When she examined him, she realized he was not the son she had borne. She figured it out by looking at him, not because anyone admitted a thing.

She says the living baby is hers: “the living one is my son and the dead one is your son.” That's the exact opposite of what the first woman said. The first woman insists right back, “No, the dead one is yours and the living one is mine.” Two women, one baby, and zero budging.

She says the dead one belongs to the first woman, not to her. Her words are “the living one is my son and the dead one is your son.” Claiming the living baby is the whole fight. If she'd claimed the dead one, there'd be no argument to bring to the king.

Nobody says anything about a sick baby here. The whole argument is about one living son and one who died. The other woman says, “the living one is my son and the dead one is your son.” There are only two babies in this fight, and only one of them is alive.

Solomon, Israel's king, says, “Bring me a sword.” Then they bring him one (1 Kings 3:24). It's a shocking thing to ask for in that moment. If it were me, I'd have asked for a long sit-down and a cookie, so there's a reason he's the king and I'm a stamper.

No elders show up in this passage. Solomon, Israel's king, doesn't call anyone in to weigh in. He has two women and two stories, and he asks for one thing: “Bring me a sword.” It's a surprise, and the surprise is part of the story.
No scroll comes out in this passage. Solomon, Israel's king, makes this request: “Bring me a sword.” He asks for a sword, not a scroll.

That's what he says: “Cut the living child in two and give half to one and half to the other.” It's a hard thing to hear, and I think the whole room felt it. Keep listening, because the story isn't done with what this order does.

He really does give this order. The king says, “Cut the living child in two and give half to one and half to the other.” It sounds shocking, and I think it's meant to land that way. Stay with it, because what happens next matters.

explanations.answer: Give the baby to the other woman
explanations.explanation: Yes. She says, “Please, my lord, give her the living baby. Do not kill him!” She'd rather lose him than see him hurt. The text says she spoke because she yearned with compassion for her son.

explanations.answer: Let the two of them share him
explanations.explanation: She doesn't ask to share. She says, “Please, my lord, give her the living baby. Do not kill him!” She asks that the other woman be given the baby and that he not be killed. Sharing him isn't what she asks for.

explanations.answer: Give her time to find a witness
explanations.explanation: She doesn't ask for time. She says, “Please, my lord, give her the living baby. Do not kill him!” There's no mention of a witness in her words. Her plea is that he not be killed.

The text says she “…yearned with compassion for her son.” That word explains why she says, “give her the living baby. Do not kill him!” Her plea is all about him staying alive. That's a mother's love in plain view.
The text doesn't say pride. It says she “…yearned with compassion for her son.” Pride would be holding on to win the argument. Her words are, “give her the living baby. Do not kill him!”

Anger isn't what the text gives her. It says she “…yearned with compassion for her son.” You can hear it in what she says: “Please, my lord…” and “Do not kill him!” Those are the words of someone pleading, not someone fighting.

explanations.answer: Neither of us gets him so cut him
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what she says: “He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!” Set that beside the other woman's plea, “Do not kill him!” Two women hear the same sword and give two completely different answers. I think that contrast is the whole moment.

explanations.answer: Put the sword away and let us go
explanations.explanation: She doesn't ask for the sword to go away. She says, “He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!” She's the one pushing the sword forward. The woman asking for mercy is the other one.

explanations.answer: Then she can leave my house for good
explanations.explanation: She says nothing about the house or about sending anyone away. Her words are “He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!” It's all about the baby and the sword. I think the room got very quiet after that.

explanations.answer: The woman who begged to spare him
explanations.explanation: Solomon says, “Give the living baby to the first woman. By no means should you kill him; she is his mother.” She's the one who said, “Do not kill him!” The king's whole ruling points at her. His ruling gives the baby to the woman who begged for his life.

explanations.answer: The woman who said to cut him
explanations.explanation: No, the baby doesn't go to her. She's the one who said, “He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!” Solomon says, “By no means should you kill him; she is his mother.” And the woman he calls his mother is the one who begged for his life.
The king's household isn't who he names. Solomon says, “Give the living baby to the first woman.” His ruling names the first woman, not the palace. And he says, “she is his mother.”

Not in his ruling. Solomon says, “Give the living baby to the first woman. By no means should you kill him; she is his mother.” The sword was an order that got a reaction out of both women. The ruling itself is the opposite of cutting.

That's right. In his ruling, Solomon says, “By no means should you kill him; she is his mother.” He rules that the baby be given to the woman who begged for his life. The sword order came first, and then the ruling said the opposite.

That's not how the people take it. The text says, “When all Israel heard of the judgment the king had given, they stood in awe of him…” Awe is a long way from thinking he was too harsh. They heard what he did and respected him for it.

Right, they don't think he's too harsh. The text says, “When all Israel heard of the judgment the king had given, they stood in awe of him…” Awe is the reaction the text gives them. It doesn't give any complaint.

The text says they saw that “…the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice.” It's the people's own conclusion about Solomon. They didn't just see a clever king. They saw wisdom from God at work in how he judged.
No army is mentioned in this verse. The people saw that “…the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice.” The only weapon the passage mentions is a sword that Solomon calls for.
Wrath isn't what they saw. The text says, “…the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice.” The people looked at his judgment and saw wisdom.
